answer: In node2vec, breadth-first sampling (small return/in-out parameter q, i.e., biased toward nodes at distance 1 from the source) restricts sampled neighborhoods to the immediate vicinity of the source node. Because the sampled nodes are structurally similar and drawn from a tightly local set, the estimate of the neighborhood's distribution has lower variance across sampled walks, giving a more stable characterization of local structural (homophily/structural-equivalence-related) roles. The limitation is that BFS-style local neighborhoods cannot capture the wider, global structure of the network: it sees only a small, overlapping set of nearby nodes and so cannot reveal macro-level position or community-distant roles. DFS, by contrast, explores deeper into the graph and can capture these broader, global structural relationships (more homophily-based community or longer-range dependencies), though at the cost of higher variance in the sampled neighborhoods.
